utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, everyone in and around the courtroom. This is case number IT-08-91-T, the Prosecutor versus Mico Stanisic and Stojan Zupljanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning to all. Before I call for the appearances, I note for the record that we again resume today under the provisions of Rule 15 bis due to the continued illness of Judge Harhoff.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. Joanna Korner and Crispian Smith on behalf of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of the Defence for Mico Stanisic, Slobodan Cvijetic and Eugene O'Sullivan. My colleague, Mr. Zecevic, will be with us a little later on.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. For the Zupljanin Defence, Igor Pantelic, Dragan Krgovic, and Katarina Danicic our case manager.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, while we're waiting for the witness to come in, is it Your Honour's intention to have a sort of procedural, as it were, conference if the witness finishes, say, an hour before the end of the session? That was the original suggestion, I know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, that's my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: And we have your list of issues.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir. Before I invite Mr. Krgovic to continue his cross-examination, I remind you that you're still on your oath.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, sir. Yesterday, before we broke for the day, we were discussing a document, so might we have it up on e-court again. 2D020609 is the number. Your Honours, I have to inform the Trial Chamber that the document still has not been translated, unfortunately, so I only have a copy in B/C/S. I'll do my best during the cross-examination to use it as little as possible, to refer to it as little as possible. I might be dealing with perhaps four or five sentences that I will read out to the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have page 2 of this document up on our screens, please. Chapter 7, may we zoom in to Chapter 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Chapter 7 is titled "The Security of Prisoners of War," or "Security for Prisoners of War," and it goes on to say who is considered to be a POW; right?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It says --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, do the interpreters -- do you know whether the interpreters have a copy of the document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: No, but I can help, give one copy.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Apart from the category that you mentioned yesterday in response to a question from the Prosecution about persons wearing uniforms and bearing arms, in addition to those, it says, "members of volunteer detachments within the armed forces." Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And also "members of resistance movements and volunteer detachments." Right?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Then members of regular armed forces of a government not recognised by the adversary; right?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And, finally, civilians or, rather, members of crews of military planes, correspondents, various suppliers, members of cultural and educational teams linked to the army, members of the navy and civil aviation, or, and this is what I'm particularly interested in, members of the population rising up to fight the enemy and locate it on free territory.

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see that on that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It's on the following page, Witness. I apologise for not telling you. At the top there, top of the page. Is that what it says in this document?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And I think you'll agree with me when I say that persons from this category, apart from the narrow definition of a POW that you discussed, was at Manjaca, too, during the time you were there, so these others?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I took the definition from the Conventions -- Geneva Conventions on Prisoners of War. It's difficult to remember it word for word. But, anyway, our regulations expanded on that concept somewhat here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Secondly, in paragraph 4 of this same document, it talks about stations for collecting prisoners of war, and they are in the rear; that is to say, centres or stations where prisoners of war are brought in from the combat zones. Is that what this means?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what this means.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And the next sentence says that prisoner of war camps shall be determined by organisation and formation or establishment; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And within the camp command, there is the established unit of a military police there to provide security?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and that was the case at Manjaca too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: That was the case at Manjaca too, you say. So there was this organisation, an establishment, and a military police unit deployed and engaged in providing security; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Now, in the third paragraph from the bottom, it says that the camp command of the POWs will decide upon the way the prisoners are distributed and housed in the camp. It also provides for a system of security for the POW camp; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And that was what was done at Manjaca; right?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. At Manjaca, we had security. The engineers provided security. We had technical security and physical security, the manpower, the people, the guards manning the observation points, and so on. And the engineer security -- technical security meant wire fences, minefields. That came under the engineers or what we called technical security for a camp or any other facilities for which security is provided.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Furthermore, in the last paragraph on that same page, it says that the prisoners of war, upon their arrest, must be evacuated away from the front-line to ensure their safety and security; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now have the following page pulled up of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Here, it speaks about escorting prisoners of war, the procedure in which prisoners of war are escorted. That's Chapter 6. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now may we have the next page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And would you focus on the second paragraph from the bottom, which is underlined on that next page. May we zoom in to that, please, on our screens. And this paragraph deals with the escort of prisoners of war on foot and the way in which they are escorted in columns, and the security provided for that column or columns. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Now, when the Prosecutor asked you earlier on about transport or the arrival of a column of POWs from Kljuc who were brought in on foot, that is nothing unusual, right, nothing out of the ordinary or in contravention to the Geneva Conventions or the rules that were applied in 1992 regarding the transport of prisoners of war on foot?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. All I said was that when we lacked motor vehicles, trucks, they went on foot, but I didn't say that that was anything unusual because at military police training sessions and courses we dealt with the escort of prisoners of war on foot many times, precisely in the way as it is set out here in this paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And since the distance from Kljuc to Manjaca is a relatively short distance, then that could be done that way; right?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it could be done that way, because I said it was just a distance of some 15 kilometres. I never calculated the distance, but I know that there's a short-cut that is even shorter, so most probably they took that short-cut.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And now in the second part of that paragraph, it says that during transport, interrogated prisoner of war officers from soldiers should be separated so that the officers should not be able to wield any influence on the subordinates and soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. During this transport on foot, the persons interrogated from persons not yet interrogated are separated, as are officers from the rank and file.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And the prisoners of war, if possible, are interrogated straight away, right, as soon as they are captured, and if they haven't been interrogated, then that is left to a later stage?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Usually it's done straight away for intelligence reasons, because the information is freshest in their minds. If you interrogate somebody straight away, they'll be able to provide you with the best information because it's fresh in their minds. And then the interrogation is continued in greater detail in the camps or elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we go back a moment to the previous page. I'd like us to look at the last and penultimate paragraph. Could we zoom in there, please. To the right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In the second paragraph there, it says that for the escort of a larger number of POWs, men are assigned from other units to carry out that task; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely, from other units. During our training courses and sessions, we mostly had cases where, when we had a large number of prisoners, men from other units were used who did not belong to the military police, for instance.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And the unit command taking part in the capture can also deploy MUP forces to provide escort for the POWs; right?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see that it says that here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But in practice, is that possible, and did that happen?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember any such case, but quite possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You said, in response to the Prosecution, that the POWs were sometimes brought in by the military police?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Now, please, take a look at the fourth paragraph from the bottom. I'm going to read out the paragraph. It says: "In cases where a person who is being escorted happens to be killed or dies a natural death along the way, or in any other way, the leader of the patrol shall inform the military police unit thereof, the nearest military prosecutor, the investigating judge of the Military Court, and the SUP, and will provide security for the site so that an on-site investigation team can arrive and launch an investigation." Do you agree that that's what it says there?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And in case in the camp, itself, a killing or death occurs of a POW, those same measures will be applied, right, in practice? And I'm referring to the case that happened involving Filipovic and that other man, the other prisoner, who succumbed to the wounds from their beatings. The military prosecutor was informed thereof, as was the Military Court. The site was secured, and the investigating judge came to carry out an on-site investigation; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we now have Exhibit P411.32 up on our screens, please. Your Honours, I'm just going to ask for the previous document to be MFI'd until we receive the translation thereof.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It's Exhibit 2D32 marked for identification, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please see the second page of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please read this document carefully first, and then I'll ask you a couple of questions regarding it. Just this text which is at the bottom. This is, in fact, a note, and it refers to the POWs who died of asphyxia during transportation to Manjaca. One may conclude from this document that notice was sent about this to the Court in Sanski Most, as well as the SUP, who was invited to carry out an on-site examination, and that a medical team examined the victims to establish the cause of death; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I deduce from this document. I didn't say yesterday that they died of this or that. They were just found dead when they arrived at the camp, and I don't know what happened before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Well, if you see that both the investigating judge and the SUP were notified that an examination was carried out by a medical team, is that fully consistent with the regulation and the rule that I read previously to you about the procedure to be applied when somebody dies of natural causes, by accident, or in another way? So the procedure in this case was fully complied with; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, do we have a date on this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: And is it --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, if we go back to the previous page of this document, I showed this document to Witness Draganovic, who confirmed that this document refers particularly to this incident. He was the president of the Court, and he -- if you remember, and he was the one who located this document at the Sanski Most Clinic or Centre and confirmed its authenticity, and he linked this document to the death of these people from Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: What's the time-frame from this investigation to the killings, themselves?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I was able to elicit from the Witness Draganovic, the one immediately followed the other. And I also asked the protected witness who used to work for the police in Sanski Most about this document, and we established the time-frame, and there was confirmation of that. I cannot tell you now exactly what page in the transcript this was stated in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Has this witness any knowledge about this, about when this investigation was conducted?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honours, this witness doesn't know what happened next. My question was purely about the fact whether, in this particular instance, the procedure that was prescribed by the rules was applied.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: The witness couldn't answer that if he doesn't know when this investigation is conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I just asked him theoretically, without specifying any time-frame, whether it is consistent with the rules to apply such a procedure and whether this procedure was complied with, and it is connected with a specific incidents other witnesses spoke about, and I think Witness Draganovic confirmed the identity of the persons who were suffocated during the transportation to Manjaca. That was this particular instance. What I asked today was only whether it was in compliance with the rules.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, the Prosecutor asked you yesterday about the witness -- sorry, not the witness, about an individual. And in that context can we please see Exhibit P481. It's a statement. You were asked whether, from the statement that you saw, it seems that he was a POW who took part in an armed insurgency, and you answered that on the basis of this document, you cannot answer that question; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we now please see Exhibit P483.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at the second paragraph from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, the previous witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. No, the --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. Sorry, can we go into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We can go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: In open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: One can see from this paragraph that the witness or, rather, the man that you questioned said that Asim Egrlic had given a weapon to Omer Filipovic, and that he took part in the arming of a Muslim unit; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And that, in fact, could have been a reason for him to be qualified as a participant in insurgency and the reason for his incarceration; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You spoke extensively about a large number of POWs who were interrogated and whose statements were taken. Generally speaking, you cannot remember each individual case, at least not the majority, with the exception of some specific and characteristic cases?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, you were asked by the Prosecutor about Dr. Sabanovic, whether you knew if he was an extremist, and you said that you didn't know whether he could be qualified as an extremist. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you know --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, that's an inaccurate answer; it's not what the witness said. I think you better find the page in the transcript. And that wasn't the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I remember the question being, Would you describe Sabanovic as an extremist? Well, in any case, the answer was negative.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it was either negative, or I think I said I didn't perceive him as such. I can't remember exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was just an introduction to my next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you know that Dr. Sabanovic was interrogated in Manjaca about the circumstances relating to his capacity of a medical doctor and that, during the conflicts in Croatia and Bosnia, issued over 2.000 false medical certificates that would assist conscripts to avoid mobilisation or to become draft-dodgers, actually?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And do you know that military investigating organs questioned, before the outbreak of the conflict, Dr. Sabanovic in Sanski Most about these circumstances?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really know nothing about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The fact is, but I am saying again hypothetically, that if it turned out that he had issued so many false certificates, that would constitute a crime and would be contrary to military laws, and that would mean assisting armed insurgents; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, in your evidence you spoke something about how the camp was set up. The camp was set up - and can you please just repeat. I think you already told us that. Can you tell us whether the camp and was set up in compliance with the military rules applicable at the time in the territory of Republika Srpska? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can the witness please be shown exhibit marked 10217 under 65 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, you asked the witness whether issuing so many false certificates, which would constitute a crime and would be contrary to military laws, that that would mean assisting armed insurgents; is that right? And the witness answers, Yes. Would you ask the witness how this would assist armed insurgents, writing certificates for people who don't want to be armed and listed?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, I'll do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, when the conflict broke out in the former Yugoslavia, the JNA declared partial mobilisation and started sending summons to conscripts either to join the army or to respond to mobilisation. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: What follows was an en-masse response by the Serbs, while the Croats and the others tried to evade receiving the summons for serving in the army and for mobilisation. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember them doing that in every possible way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: One of the ways was to have a false medical certificate that they were not fit for military service.

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was one of the ways.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: On the other hand, those persons who failed to respond to mobilisation in the JNA joined paramilitary formations for the Croat and Muslim forces that were in the process of being formed at the time; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And in that manner, the combat power of the JNA, and later of Republika Srpska forces, were weakened?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I said. The defence capacity of the armed forces of the country were weakened, and under the law this included fleeing from the armed forces, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And in that way, they directly assisted armed insurgents against the JNA and later against Republika Srpska and the legal system of the SFRY?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it could be interpreted in that manner. This affected the capacity of the forces that were preparing insurgency.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like this document not be broadcast, because I don't know if it is a confidential one. Maybe my learned friend can help me. Does it fall into the category that should not be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It hasn't been broadcast, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know if the Prosecutor showed you this document during proofing or if you had an opportunity to see it at some earlier stage. It's the minutes of the meeting at Manjaca between the POW camp commander that took place on the 31st of August, 1992. So can you please look at page 2 of this document. In the English, it is on page 1 and continues onto page 2, the conversations. We have certain notes and observations by the camp commander. I'll go through some of those observation to ask you whether they correspond to the actual situation on the ground in Manjaca at that time. He introduces himself first and explains what type of camp it is. And then in paragraph 4 or item 4, he says that in conformity with Article 2 of the Geneva Conventions, paragraph 78 and 90, he and the prisoners elected their representatives and deputy representatives. So I'm asking you now whether, in Manjaca, did the prisoners elect their deputies or representatives, in fact, and how did that function in Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. A commissioner for the entire camp was Captain Vahid Ceric, who was the same man mentioned on that statement we looked at yesterday, and each pavilion had one representative or commissioner or deputy representing them, the prisoners. And through that person, the prisoners could address their rights.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 5, the colonel -- or, rather, Colonel Popovic says that the people in the camp were caught in the combat zone and that that was done in conformity with Articles 4 of the Geneva Conventions, number 1 and 2, A, B, C, and D, which specify who can be a POW.

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: As far as I understand it, this -- your testimony is only correct in part, because you said that you received information from the prisoners of war, themselves, and that some of them were not captured in the combat zone. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. On the basis of the investigations we conducted -- the interrogation we conducted, they mostly said that they were captured at home or working out in the fields, and you had no other information, so it was difficult to establish what had actually happened. And from the notes coming in from the ground, they said otherwise, so it was different to make a judgement and conclude what had actually happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Because you didn't have reliable information; they said one thing, some witnesses said another, and the notes came in from the Serb authorities, if I can call them that, they said something else, so you had no reliable proof and evidence that they were actually prisoners of war; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But, at any rate, when those people were captured and brought in, it was your duty to investigate, to interrogate them and see whether they were actually prisoners of war or not?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We didn't have time. Let me say this straight away. We didn't have time to interrogate everybody and investigate, because there were 4.403 persons, so we would need much more time than we had to question all of them. Now, for those who were accompanied by a note, and we had a note about them, we interrogated them only superficially; briefly, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And what it says here or follows on from this report, he says that the conditions in the camp were not ideal, that they were lacking in hygiene and medical assistance. And what I would like -- or what I can see from this document and what I can understand from your testimony, you did your best, given the prevailing conditions and circumstances, to ensure the best possible conditions for the prisoners?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have nothing to add or subtract. We did our best. I, personally, was happy to see that most people understood -- well, that the camp commanders understood the situation, and the people that had arrived and were alive in the camp should leave in the same way.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And the status and conditions in the camp were affected by objective circumstances. First of all, there was a war in the area, in the region, a war nearby, right, in proximity to the camp, and the fact that this part was isolated from Republika Srpska and the rest of the country for a period of time?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that I was going to add without you having to ask me. The situation was a very difficult one at the time. We were cut off from the rest of Republika Srpska and from Serbia, itself. The corridor had been intercepted. You know that 12 babies died in Banja Luka for lack of oxygen, and the logistics was a great problem for supplies. So we had to send POWs to our logistics base in Banja Luka or, rather, they sent as much food as they could. We told them of the numbers we had, but they sent the same amount of bread and food as they sent to the combatants up at the front-lines, and that was very little to begin with.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And the situation improved, did it, when the corridor was broken through sometime in July 1992 and when the International Red Cross Committee began to come in and distribute food and help the POWs generally; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, the situation improved significantly, and the Merhamet also stepped in to help, the charity from Banja Luka. The ICRC from Geneva did, too, in July, and the situation improved quite significantly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 7, what the camp commander says there, as far as the conditions in the camp were concerned, he says: "We did everything we could in order to comply with part 2 of Articles 22 to 27 of the Geneva Conventions." He says: "I would have been happier to have been able to accommodate them in hotels, but I didn't have that possibility." So under the given circumstances, everything possible was done?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and I'd like to ask everybody dealing with this issue to bear in mind the time and the context in which the camp existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So on your part, and the camp administration, beginning with the commander, et cetera, it was never their intention -- or, rather, these POWs were not intentionally faced with a food shortage or difficult living conditions; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, precisely. Nobody -- I never experienced anybody in the chain of command, from the Presidency of Republika Srpska down to the last guard, that any of those people ever had the intention of making life difficult for the POWs or people coming into the camp by keeping them hungry or trying to liquidate them in any shape or form.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please read the other paragraphs on page 2 of the document, paragraphs 4 to 11. Could you look through those, please, so that I can move on.

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've read them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Could you now move on to page 3 of this document, please. On that page, would you take a look at paragraph 15. Mr. Popovic refers, in that paragraph, to some of the deaths that occurred in the POW camp. Now, does that paragraph correspond to what you know about what happened at Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have to take a moment to look at this in greater detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we zoom in to paragraph 15, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, here the camp commander says that there were six deaths, and I think -- well, I know for certain that that's a mistake, because there were five deaths, of which three were natural deaths and the other two violent deaths of the type that I described yesterday. So not six, but five.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And they didn't all die a natural death. Two of them died as a result of violence; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: In the remaining part of that document, does it correspond to the situation in the camp?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we move on to the next page, then, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Look at that page carefully, please, and please focus on paragraph 26. And could we zoom in on paragraph 26, please. To the best of your recollections, do those figures correspond to the ones you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't want to do any math here, but everybody over the age of 60 and under the age of 18, and any sick persons, and I think there were 82 of those, were sent for treatment, and the others were released through Merhamet, so that would roughly be the right figure. But he didn't mention the number of exchanged persons. So an exchange took place, and it was a river that flowed continuously, new people coming in and other people being exchanged. So in the course of a week, there was always one exchange process taking place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: May we move on to the next page. Well, you've looked at the rest of the page, and that corresponds to the situation in the camp on the ground; right?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Now let's see the next page. And would you focus on paragraph 33 there, please, where it says that there was a period where an investigation -- an interrogation period was conducted, everybody was interrogated, and if it was proved that they did not take part in the fighting, they would be released. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that is what happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And then in paragraph 36, Colonel Popovic says: "I would have been very happy if I were in a possibility to fulfill all the conditions stipulated under the Geneva Conventions." So that, in fact, is a joint desire expressed by the camp commander and yourself, that you would be very happy to have been able to comply with all the Geneva Conventions stipulations; right?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And later on, further down, he says when the camp was established and under whose command it is. And moving on to the next page, he says that the camp was under the control of the Army of Republika Srpska and -- well, Republika Srpska; right?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Now may we focus on law and order in the camp. And you said the conditions more or less correspond to your impressions; right?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: May we go on to the next page, please. In paragraph 39 --

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Forty-nine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I apologise. I need the previous page. An expert in nutrition was due to arrive to establish the camp requirements and to establish the aid needed by the ICRC. Do you remember that a nutritionist came into Manjaca and that after his visit the quantity and quality of food improved?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A nutritionist was there every day from 9.00 to 5.00 p.m. She was there with an interpreter. She walked freely around the camp without anybody's control, police or otherwise. And this took place at the end of July and went on to the end of September or, rather, for as long as the camp was in existence. And after that, the food improved significantly. And thanks to the ICRC, which brought in food in trailers from Zagreb on a daily basis, the situation improved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Let's move back to page 3 to look at paragraph 12, please. That addresses POWs and their work activities, and it says that under Articles 50 and 51 of the Geneva Conventions, the conditions of work are stipulated; that is to say, that POWs did not take part in trench-digging or were not supposed to be exposed to dangerous conditions in the war zone, and that, in principle, there was less work for the POWs to do than they were willing to do.

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The POWs from Manjaca, not a single one were used for war purposes, that is to say, digging trenches, setting up human shields, or anything like that, but just for socially-beneficial work, and this was on a voluntary basis. And, in fact, more POWs volunteered to go out and do work than were actually required and used.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have finished with that document now, please, so may it be given an exhibit number, if there are no objections?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can I just go back to the last document, the manual, for a moment. Obviously, we're at a disadvantage, as we -- I imagine you have no idea what any of this says. But is this -- could we confirm that this is all part of one manual, both sections?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, the document is already an exhibit in the Popovic trial, and I can provide it to you. I can bring the integral text, the integral manual, so you can have a look at it. It would be difficult for me to locate just that portion. I think we have it in the library downstairs. But I'll bring in the entire manual. That's why I asked that it be marked for identification. Once it's been translated, you can see the whole thing.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'd be very grateful for the whole manual, if that's possible. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So the current application is for the admission into -- the present document having been tendered and entered as an exhibit.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit 2D33, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The Prosecutor showed you a set of documents in which you described individual incidents that took place in the POW camp and its surroundings. You recorded them meticulously, and you reacted to them. Now, what I would like to say to you, I'm talking about five or six documents describing these incidents. However, beyond these reports of yours, I have an impression that these were isolated incidents that were responded to and an action was taken in accordance with the Rules of Service, at least by yourself?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, exactly. Whatever I learned about and what I thought was either illegal or contrary to the rules, I recorded that and reported that, but not for the purpose of reporting alone, but for responding to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And outside of the reports that you wrote, no other incidents took place, or maybe you don't know about them?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know about them. If I had known, I would have written about them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Bearing in mind these incidents in the prisoners of war camp, the expression that we heard in this court, such as "concentration camp" or "death camp" or "killing camp," is rather untrue; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. We were attacked very much for the very word "camp." I think that in our rules and regulations, even in the ones we've seen today, there was a rule which provided that for housing POWs, one needs to set up a camp. Now, if someone is confusing a concentration camp with a POW camp, it's not our fault. We even had an inscription in the camp which says that this was a POW camp. No one can ever call it a death camp, because 4.403 prisoners went through this camp. There were only five deaths. Two of them were violent deaths, and three were the deaths caused by natural causes. If you, on that basis, can call this camp a death camp, then these are people who are entertaining prejudices.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, the Manjaca camp, if compared according to the information that you had about the POWs from the Serbian side or the Muslim side or coming from other centres, the Manjaca camp in the area of Bosnia-Herzegovina and Croatia, where there was war, I think that in that camp one can say that the conditions are best.

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If we compared this camp that I have knowledge about, and one can freely say that if we try to measure the level of regularity in the camp, the Manjaca camp can be qualified as the most regular and regulated ones. This might sound strange to someone.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreters note, could the witness and counsel please speak more slowly and pause between questions and answers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The interpreters are reminding you, Mr. Krgovic, and the witness to allow an interval to facilitate the translation.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours, you're right. Due to this overlapping, there is no distinction in the transcript between the question and answer. So please be patient with me. It was my mistake. I was too hasty in putting the question. So from page 26, line 6, is where the answer begins, after the words "if you compare this camp that I have knowledge about." So this is where the witness's answer begins, and before that was my question. I apologise to the interpreters and the Chamber. I will do my best to slow down, not because time is elapsing, but I will try to bring this to an end as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, you said that as far as you know, the majority of the POWs had been brought by the police, but you didn't have information at that time who arrested or captured them; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't have that information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm going to show you now a document which is Exhibit 5390.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: P390.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, it's my mistake. I apologise to the interpreters. I didn't pronounce the first word quite clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, I don't think that you had an opportunity to see this document. Therefore, I kindly ask you to look at it or, rather, item D of this document. But before that, can we look at page 2 to see who signed this document. You can see that this was signed by the chief of the Public Security Station, Mirko Vrucinic. This was the SJB in Sanski Most; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: You have heard of him, but you never met him?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. This is what is written here. I don't know anything about this document because it had been drafted before I came to Manjaca and Banja Luka --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: This was the 5th of August, 1992. Let's go back to page 1 now, please. So let's go back to page 1.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm just going to interrupt for a moment, because the witness says he's never seen the document before, he doesn't know about the contents, what's he supposed to say about it, other than, I can see what's written?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm going to show to the witness only one paragraph of this document, and this is already an exhibit. I was just going to ask the witness whether he's aware of the fact contained in this single paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes. Please proceed, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please look at paragraph D. In this paragraph, it says that: "In combat operations or so-called clearing operations, the army picks up the population (of late only persons fit for military service), and simply hands them over to the civilian organs and authorities. After that, the police are obliged to provide security for these camps, and as part of that, are responsible for food, health-care, hygiene, and the like." Sir, just one question. Do you know that in those operations in combat zones, military units herded the population and brought them in, the population that was in a combat zone?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, yes. I would like for us to stand corrected. I didn't know that this was August. I was there in June. What you asked me about, whether I knew if that was being done and that these people were handed over to the police, in principle I know that that was the procedure that was applied.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please now look at Exhibit P382.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, before we see this document on our screens, you mentioned that during the take-over these prisoners were brought in by the police. In fact, you were the one who received all the notes and the lists from the policemen who escorted the transports; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And now I'm going to show you a document relating to the transportation to Manjaca, and it speaks about who is taking part in that. I kindly ask you to read this document carefully. You can see here who is providing escort for the POWs. The second sentence reads: "Three members of the prison premises, three members of the Public Security Station, and four members of the military police provided escort." Do you know, and I underline "do you know," whether military police and security guards of the camp took part in escort?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I didn't give you a decisive answer either yesterday or today, which is that in all cases the POWs were escorted by the police. However, when we had to deal with a large number of POWs who were moved from one camp to another, they normally came escorted by the police. However, when we had smaller groups coming from the front, which is to say, genuine fresh POWs, they were brought in by the military police, and they provided escort during transportation. So I don't rule out that these were also military policemen at the head of the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday, in response to the Prosecutor's question, and the Prosecutor showed you a document about the release of persons under the age of 18 and over 60, at one point you said that a group of prisoners was handed over to the Merhamet because they were the only ones ready to receive them. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: The problem that you highlighted in a few of your reports with the release of these categories of people for whom it has been established that were under the ages of 18 and over the age of 60, had no place to return to for various reasons?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, and that was a problem.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: From what I could see from various documents, the problem with them was because some of them had been living and had residence in the houses that were still in the areas where combat operations were in progress?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And, secondly, due to war operations or due to the clearing of the terrain, some of their houses were ruined; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were cases like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And they had no place to return to?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please slow down. And it's 10.25, so if this is a convenient point, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We'll resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, while the witness is coming in, one of the documents that Mr. Krgovic showed, he asked me whether it should be under seal. That's the conversation with Colonel Popovic. It's been an exhibit in previous trials, and I am not, at this stage, sure whether it was under seal or not. It's because of the provider. Can I just, for safety's sake, I think, at this stage say that that document, whatever the number was, should be under seal, and if it was all right to have it not under seal, well, then we'll come back to you on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I was informed by Defence counsel that Exhibit 2D33 should be under seal.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, well, that's the one we're [microphone not activated]... discussing, but I'm not sure about that, that's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I think that's a preferable course. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Before you begin, Mr. Krgovic, I would again respectfully remind you to bear in mind the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I'll do my best, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, I'll continue where we left off before the break. Let me remind you, I was talking about the reasons for which there were problems for persons under the age of 18 and over the age of 60 to be released from the POW camp, and I listed some of the reasons why this was sometimes difficult, reasons that I read from relevant documents. So I'd like you to confirm or not confirm this, or you've already done that. Anyway, the area from which these POWs came in from, to a large extent, was void of the population because the population had left certain areas because of combat, and that's where these POWs were coming from; right?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So in that area, there was a lot of insecurity because of some groups that were rampant in the area, so it was a threat to their security to stay on in those places; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And what happened was, in many cases, that some people would be released, they went to areas of this kind, and they were either abused there or killed there. That happened, too; right?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So all that constituted the reasons for which -- among other reasons, of course, for which their release was prolonged, which took a long -- for which it took a long time to have them to be released from the camp; right?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Now, you also spoke about the fact that in the POW camp, there were a number of imams, religious figures?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think there were four imams and a priest, a friar.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And they were released among the first lot, although it was established, in actual fact, that some of them had taken part in combat and bore arms; right?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was some information to that effect, that a hodja, I don't know which one -- that an automatic rifle was found on a hodja in a mosque. But as far as these religious personnel were concerned, the decision was made to release them, and I think they were released and handed over to the main imam in Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May we have Exhibit P484 shown to the witness now, please, and put up on our screens.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Look at the last paragraph there, please. And can we zoom in to it. That's your report, is it not?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: And these religious persons are described here, one of whom had a weapon in a mosque, and another pulled out an automatic weapon from a vehicle, et cetera, et cetera, as it says here. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says clearly there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: One of the reasons why everything was running late in this respect was that for those people under the age of 18 and over the age of 60 and the sick, it was established that they, in fact, possessed weapons and had taken part in combat, so an abolition needed to be gone through there; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. President Karadzic abolished those people that had to go elsewhere for treatment, so an act on abolition was passed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Now another question. When describing your activities, you said that you could only propose certain measures, whether to the camp commander or your superior command, with respect to the release of people from the camp, whereas the final decision was taken by the organ that was superior to Colonel Popovic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I said, and that's how it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Right. Now look at Exhibit P489, please. Take a look at what it says at the bottom of that page, the signature and everything else. And this refers to persons under the age of 18, and the decision that they can be released was okayed by Colonel Vukelic.

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Colonel Vukelic was assistant commander, co-commander for morale, and, as such, he was able to bring in a decision of this kind releasing them from the camp, giving his permission for that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Corps commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just check to see if I have anything further to raise. I apologise to the Trial Chamber for taking up time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: One more question. As far as you know, in view of the duties that you performed, after the people were released and exchanged, the POWs, from Manjaca, that immediately afterwards they took part in combat operations on the other side and that some of them were taken prisoner again and even set up some sort of 17th Knights Brigade or whatever it was called, but that they were captured again immediately upon their release from the camp because they had taken part in combat?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. With the help of the ICRC and the Serbian authorities, we released persons in three groups, the first being on the 14th of November, and the other groups were subsequently released on the 12th -- or, rather, the 14th, 16th, and 18th of December. Every other day, they were released. Groups were released every other day until the whole camp was disbanded and released. And now people were interested in hearing what had happened to these people -- I apologise, I'm speeding up, so sorry to the interpreters. Anyway, they were all supposed to go to so-called third countries, so not any of the former SFRY republics but to third countries. Mostly, they went to Germany and Belgium, where they requested to go, in fact. But in that first stage of their departure, which was Karlovac after Manjaca, many expressed the desire to go back to the Federation of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and joined up with the armed forces again there. Now, I can't remember the names and surnames of these people or how many people, but a certain number was recaptured, they were captured again. And I think they should have recalled my words, many of them, when I said that perhaps Manjaca was their salvation, because had they stayed at home, they would have perhaps been killed up at the front-line, fighting, whereas in Manjaca their lives would have been saved and were saved.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. I have no further questions for you. That completes my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, can I ask that -- the exhibit that I said if we could have under seal for caution's sake, we've checked. It wasn't under seal in the other trials, so there's no objection to it being an ordinary exhibit in the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I, Your Honours?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: Witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I think Ms. Korner's point, with which I respectfully agree, is that it is easy to draw inferences from these questions that you were asking which would result in the identification of the witness.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, you may recall the exchange I had with Mr. Cvijetic at some point, and we just remained in private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, I was just waiting. I didn't hear you say.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, you were asked by Mr. Krgovic to look at a list of what was defined as a prisoner of war in some kind of military police manual, and one of the definitions in the manual, as opposed to any of the Geneva Conventions, was: "Members of the population rising up to fight the enemy." What do you understand by the term "fight"?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot understand it otherwise than that it has to do with an armed combat.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So we're talking, are we, about somebody armed with a weapon, carrying out combat, if you like, against, in this case, the Army of the Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's so. Our Law on the All People's Defence envisaged a transition from wartime to wartime system; therefore, a state of war. And "combat," as you put it, or "fight" could be slightly different. "Fighting" means fighting with weapons. However, taking part in a war can also involve companies or enterprises continuing their operation during the war for the purposes of war efforts.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I want you to have a look, please, again at the document you saw yesterday, which is now Exhibit P487. I remind you of what you told the Court yesterday, in relation to this report, that they are being brought in massively, in large quantities, particularly from Kljuc and Sanski Most, bringing in those who shouldn't be treated as prisoners of war because they've been picked up from their homes and off their fields, and individuals who are older than 60 and younger than 18. When you wrote those words, as you told the Court they were true, do those persons, in your view, come within the definition of fighting persons?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wrote it in that way because I perceived it in that way through interviews with them. I had no other documents at my disposal. I found out, according to their statements, that they had been picked up from their houses following an invitation for them to assemble at a certain point. I wrote this in order to give an incentive to the command to cease such a practice, particularly because we were again receiving people under the age of 18 and over the age of 60. This is why I wrote this in this way.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we go into private session for a moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I've only got about another -- well, if you feel we ought to take the break. But can I, for the purposes of the end of this, say that I've only got about another 10 minutes' worth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So we'll resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, may I just note for the purposes of the transcript that I've been joined by Ms. Pidwell on behalf of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, you were asked questions about Dr. Sabanovic which arose out of the questions that you were asked by me in chief; namely, whether Dr. Sabanovic, who was on the list of the most radical extremists in the area of Sanski Most, and I asked you, just so we get the exact quote, page 5278 of the transcript: "Was there anything about his conversations or anything about what you learned about him to suggest that he was, as described, the most radical -- one of the most radical extremists?" And you said: "Not that I could see." And you were then asked whether you knew that he had signed certificates, effectively fake certificates, exempting Muslims from conscription during the war in Croatia. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And a theory was put to you that by signing these exemption certificates, effectively he had been aiding -- I'll just get the right question, the actual question -- that he was assisting armed insurgents, which Judge Delvoie queried that. A series of propositions was put to you, ending up with this one: "On the other hand, those persons who failed to respond to mobilisation in the JNA joined the paramilitary formations for the Croat and Muslim forces." And you agreed with that. How do you know that the people who had been exempted from military service by means of these certificates all went off and joined the paramilitary formations?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All that was hypothetical, both the question and the answer, let me say. I don't have any specific information telling me that any of the people that Sabanovic released or exempted went to enemy formations, to the enemy, the adversary. But hypothetically speaking, you can deduce that and conclude that, because where would they go? But I don't have any specific information. So in answer to your question, I don't specifically have any information about anybody joining up with the enemy forces of the ones released by Sabanovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And let's return to the original topic. I don't know what's meant by "radical extremists," but as a matter of common sense it would be somebody who was espousing violent resistance to the take-over of areas by the Bosnian Serb forces. Did anything in the conversations that you had over a long period of time, some eight or so -- well, some months, with Dr. Sabanovic suggest that he was the type of person who was doing that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I object for that -- first, the basis, did this witness make conversation with Sabanovic? That was the first question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I thought it had been quite clear. All right, I'll go back.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In the period of time that Dr. Sabanovic was the doctor in the camp and formed part of the reception committee, did you have conversations with Dr. Sabanovic?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on many occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. So the original question: Anything in his conversation or anything about him to suggest that he was espousing violent resistance to the take-overs?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't have that information either from the notes -- even if there were some SUP notes about him, which there were -- I can't remember quite what they said, but apparently he gave some injections to Serb children, something that was extremely important in deducing whether he's an extremist or not. But this was information that was not substantiated with any proof or evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: My actual question is, is your personal impression of him, sir, from the many conversations that you had with him. That's what I'm asking for.

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The impression is, and according to the information that I had that--

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Forget -- all right. Yes, go on. Yes, carry on.

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I was saying, I couldn't rank him among the group of extremists. I couldn't really say he was that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, thank you. Now, next you said, when Mr. Krgovic was taking you through -- and, I'm sorry, I should have asked you this earlier. When you met Mr. Krgovic originally in Bosnia and then for a couple of hours or so on, I believe, Tuesday evening -- Wednesday evening, did you discuss -- did he discuss with you the questions that he was going to ask you?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He enumerated the topics that he would be dealing with and the rules or, rather, the rule that holds true here. He showed me that, and that's it. I don't know what else you might be referring to, what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, a number of these questions, if I can put it this way, sir, and it's a matter for the Trial Chamber, you answered fairly swiftly, without much time for pausing, and agreed with nearly every proposition that was put to you, and so I'm just wondering whether or not these were discussed with you when you met him.

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not about everything, but it was logic that it was involved here and the knowledge I had performing my duties, in the line of duty and my service for over all those years, so I don't need to think about it. That's a fact.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I want to ask you about one answer you gave when you were being shown the record of a conversation with Colonel Popovic conducted by Mr. McLeod from what was then called the European Community Monitoring Mission. And it was put to you -- a number of questions about the camp, and it was put to you that under the given circumstances, everything possible was done for the prisoners in the camp. And you said: "Yes, and I'd like to ask everybody dealing with this issue to bear in mind," although the word "bear" has been missed out from page 20, line 3, "the time and the context in which the camp and existed." "So on your part," said Mr. Krgovic, "on the camp administration beginning with the order, et cetera, it was never their intention or, rather, they were not intentionally faced with a food shortage or difficult conditions; isn't that right?" And you said: "Yes, precisely. Nobody -- I never experienced anybody in the command, from the Presidency of the Republika Srpska down to the guard, that any of these people ever had the intention of making it difficult for the prisoners of war or people coming into the camp by keeping them hungry or trying to liquidate them." Now, firstly, did you ever see any orders from the Presidency of the Republika Srpska in connection with the camps, other than the internationals being allowed in there?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: (redacted) I understood that there was nobody down the chain of command who had the aim of, let me put it this way, massive sufferance or annihilation of the people in the camp, so I didn't want to take part in a game like that either. And I even thought that if anything like that happened that I would leave, although I would be held criminally responsible, because according to the law orders which ordered you to commit crimes need not be heeded, so you could refuse to obey an order if the order involved committing a crime.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... in this part of page 66, line 9 and 10, must be redacted because --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: What was the condition of the Omarska prisoners when they arrived at Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I don't think that I raised this issue in my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It arises out of the answer that there was no, as it were, common plan to starve or make life difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But in Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's not what the witness said.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sir, what was the condition of the prisoners from Omarska when they arrived at Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They looked -- seemed under-nourished, not well cared for. And I have to add that what I was thinking of was the treatment of prisoners at Manjaca, because I never went to Keraterm or Prijedor, in that camp there, so I meant Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Well, can we just have a look then briefly, please, at one document which you've seen, but we didn't refer to it in examination-in-chief, on Manjaca, itself. Could you have a look, please, at document P179.13.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I have to object to this document and this line of questioning because this is a document from the ICRC, and I did not mention it in my cross-examination. I made no mention of any commission or any report from the ICRC, nor do I know how -- where this line of questioning is going or how this document can be used in this redirect. But if the Trial Chamber allows the Prosecutor to ask questions on this document, then I should like to ask time for additional questioning so that I, in my turn, can ask the witness about this and other documents which I also did not use.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Krgovic, sorry, opened this line of questioning through his cross-examination on the -- full cross-examination on the document of the conversation that Mr. McLeod had with Colonel Popovic, in which the colonel put his side of matters to Mr. McLeod. The conversation then moved on to the question and answer that I have just dealt with in which it is said that there was no -- anybody in command from the president of Republika Srpska down, that any of the people ever had the intention of making it difficult for the POWs or keeping them hungry. This report is directly attributable to that line of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: But if to the extent that there is a, for want of a better expression, spill-over, aren't you inviting the prolongation of this by Mr. Krgovic having to deal with -- be given leave to deal with these matters again?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Mr. Krgovic should have thought of that before he embarked on the line of questioning and should have dealt with it himself, because it was perfectly obvious that this is something that's going to be dealt with in re-examination. So the fact that he decided to ignore the document which was in our list, but because it was already at that exhibit I went over it, that's the decision he took, and he's stuck with it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please proceed, and we'll see where we go. Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. I did not deal with this document because the Prosecutor chose to ignore the document during the examination-in-chief, so that was precisely the reason why I failed to deal with it. Now, if you allow the Prosecutor to ask questions about this document which he or she intentionally side-stepped during in-chief, then I'd like to ask questions about this and two other documents linked to this document. But because of the shortage of time and because the Prosecutor did not deal with it during the examination-in-chief, I did not address the matter in cross-examination either.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, sorry, can I respond?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Just a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You wanted to respond, Ms. --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, this document is already an exhibit in the case. The fact that, through reasons of timing, I didn't deal with it personally with this witness is one thing. But if Defence counsel deliberately adopts a line of questioning which could be said to be misleading - and in our submission is because he concentrated on the conversation that Mr. McLeod had with Colonel Popovic, and Your Honour will hear about that, from the witness at a later date - he can't then complain if a document that's already an exhibit in the case and which has been looked at is then referred to in re-examination to correct a misleading impression. And shouldn't be allowed, I'm afraid, in our submission, to have another go at it. He took the decision, only to put it -- ask about that document and not about the document that says the very opposite.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please proceed, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Might I just be allowed to respond, and I'll sit down. The witness, when he was shown the document here, it was a document criticising that -- well, he said that the document was biased and did not contain all the facts. And my line of questioning would be to show the witness this document and the document that he wrote in which he speaks about this first document. That's all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Whatever tactical reasons either side would have had for proceeding in the manner in which they have up to this point in relation to this document, in terms of the -- in order for the Chamber to have the benefit of all of the relevant evidence, I'm going to allow Ms. Korner to proceed, and I would have to, in fairness, allow Mr. Krgovic to return to this briefly. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is a document, sir, that you looked at during the course of your review of the documents in the case, and, indeed, we have already referred to the letter, and it is an exhibit that you wrote about this. However, can we look at what is said for the first time that the ICRC get to the camp. And this is letter they sent to -- it was dated the 22nd of July and was sent to the president of the republic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Can we look, please, at page 2 -- sorry, page 2, it's the third -- my fault. It's the one, two, three -- fifth page in English. It's the actual report, and it is -- it's -- I don't know. It's page 0124-6849 at the top. And we've got neither up at the moment. Oh, we actually do. I'm not sure what the English document is, but it's not -- I want the English of that, please, which is, as I say, the fourth page -- fifth page. I don't know what you've got up on there, but that's not it. The English should -- you've got the B/C/S. The English looks like that [indicates]. All right, it doesn't matter. Give me that page, I'll -- 0124-6846, please.
