utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I understand the page is not in e-court, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So I've just been told by the usher, and we're going to put it up on Sanction.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, all right. In fact, it's also -- they sent -- in the B/C/S, they sent a copy of the English paper. Do you have, in Sanction, 0124-6846? Your Honour, I'm sorry about the ten minutes, but it's going to be causing -- it's mixed in with the B/C/S, I think. It's page 6 of the B/C/S. So if we can have page -- the page we've got up already in B/C/S, plus page 6. It's all mixed up together. That's why I think it's -- right. Finally. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. This is the working paper that was sent to Mr. Karadzic. It's the visit to, paragraph 2, "Treatment." "The ICRC visit was terminated prematurely, 12.15, when delegates observed that two detainees had been subjected to ill treatment during the visit." I don't think that means they were beaten up during the visit, but just bad grammar: "All eight delegates present in camp observed on detainees frequent and widespread traces of recent and often severe beatings; those most often were fresh hematomas inflicted in a time-period since arrival at Manjaca." "3. Material conditions. General living conditions with regard to food, hygiene, clothing and accommodation," quality that must be, not qualify, "are absolutely insufficient. "Many detainees show marked weight loss and signs of anaemia with severity often corresponding to length of detention." And then it deals with the facilities. Now, sir, this visit was in July, before the Omarska prisoners or the prisoners from Keraterm arrived, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And so the signs of beatings and/or malnourishment, and the food and hygiene, related to conditions or related to people who had not come from either of those two camps?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And you told us, yourself, in your earlier testimony that there were beatings in the camp?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And even though, as you told us when we looked at your letter -- your report about this, which I think we've already exhibited -- I can't remember what the number is now, but anyhow --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Can we have that up? Perhaps we can come down the page a bit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: You said there: "As far as the beatings are concerned, that is correct, although it is hard to ascertain when they were created, whether in the camp or before their arrival, i.e., during arrest." So you accept that on that part, that report of the ICRC is accurate; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Which part, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In respect of the beatings.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but can you read the right part, because it's a leading question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I'm perfectly happy to put up any other part of the letter that Mr. Krgovic would like me to -- the report, rather. All right, can we move on? And then you've been given permission, Mr. Krgovic, in any event, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And it's right, isn't it, sir, that in July, before the ICRC arrived, the food and the hygiene and --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Objection. Leading.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you agree with the report that we've just looked at, that the general living conditions with regard to food, hygiene, clothing, accommodation, are grossly insufficient -- were grossly and absolutely insufficient?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, sir, finally on this -- on this aspect, you were asked a number of leading questions, quite properly because it's cross-examination, about the war-torn areas, if I can put that, from which some of these people came, and you seemed to agree that these people had been brought in to Manjaca because it was unsafe for them to remain in the area; in other words, they were being brought in for their own protection. Is that really what you're telling the Court, that a number of these people were being kept in this camp in these conditions for their own protection?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I emphasised that in one of my reports; that is to say, that for a number of prisoners, there was no evidence of participation, and they were brought there just to bring them to safety. That is what I put in my report, and we discussed that yesterday. As far as today's Defence examination is concerned, we spoke about the return of the prisoners under the age of 18 and over 60, and we said that it was impossible for them to return because their places of residence were already vacated, and therefore they had no place to return to. So we have two different instances. I don't know which one you're referring to in your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Let's just deal with the people, who you seem to be agreeing with, who had been picked up off the fields, taken from their homes, and brought to Manjaca. Are you saying that these people had only been brought to Manjaca for their own protection? Is that what you're saying to this Court now?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right, and that's what I put in one of my reports, and I abide by that.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And what was the justification, sir, for keeping them in a prisoner of war camp in those conditions?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not up to me to say that. I just noted that in order to encourage the decision-makers to do something in terms of either exchanging these people or releasing the prisoners. So that was the purpose of what I wrote, and that is how I understood it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I think we'd better know finally, then, sir, what you are saying. Are you saying that in your opinion, it was proper procedure for people who had taken no part in any kind of armed rebellion to be brought to the camp and kept there for months for their own protection?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely so.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's what you say, is it, sir?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what I am saying.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, in that case, sir, I don't think I've got any further questions for you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Krgovic, when I indicated earlier that you would be allowed to return to this ICRC document, you mentioned two other documents. How do they -- how does this permission allow you to deal with these further documents?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I'm not going to deal with these two documents. I'm only going to ask a question that is relevant for that. I'm not going to show the documents to the witness. I'll just put two questions because these two documents are linked with this document. If the witness gives me an answer concerning this document, then I'm not going to ask him questions about the other two documents or, rather, I'm not going to mention these two documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Please proceed carefully one question at a time. Further cross-examination by Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, during proofing the Prosecution showed you this ICRC document; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Were you asked on that occasion what you thought about the objectivity of this report, and did you express some objections of yourself to this report?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but at the moment I cannot say for certain what I said exactly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: On that occasion, and that can be drawn as an inference from the other document shown to you, which is P490, Colonel Vukelic and -- as the camp commander, and yourself, pointed out that these allegations about the conditions were unbased and unfounded, and they promised to amend their report by incorporating your objections. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: However, they did not correct their report; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. After Vukelic's and Popovic's reactions, they did amend certain things, but that only remained orally. No written report was amended to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And these objections related to the conditions prevailing in the camp and the fact that it wasn't established when these injuries were inflicted?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Whether during the capture or in the camp itself?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And Colonel Vukelic, in his report, which was shown to you by the Prosecution, demonstrated that they didn't draft their report by adopting an unbiased approach and that they had exaggerated the conditions in Manjaca, and that was the essence of the objections raised by yourself and Colonel Vukelic?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's right, and also the context of the whole situation was not taken into account. Popovic explained that earlier, and it had been seen from this document. Quite simply, the camp and the prisoners virtually shared the destiny of the people and the military personnel at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And they did not acknowledge an objective remark that the prisoners were given everything that was possible at the time that you had at your disposal?

utterances.speaker: ST-172 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we made great efforts to improve the situation and to reach the level that would be adapted to the given situation and the time-period.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Your Honours, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. CVIJETIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, just to correct one of my mistakes, in the system of the three interconnected orders, and having to do with the same topic, the witness gave most of his answers with relation to the last one, which I didn't tender to be admitted into evidence, and the intention was to present them all together. Since you admitted into evidence the first two ones, I also tender document 1443 according to 65 ter to be admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Admitted and marked.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit 1D157, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, we thank you for your coming to assist the Tribunal, and you are now released. The usher would escort you from the courtroom, because the Chamber has other matters with which to deal before it rises. We wish you a safe journey back to your home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The Chamber is in receipt of the copy of the memorandum over the signature of Ms. Pidwell, indicating the matters -- the list of five matters, and they've consulted the Defence in terms of the content of the list. And dealing with the first item, I suppose this is the Prosecution means of alerting the Chamber that the appropriate motion will be made in due course.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No, Your Honour, it was not our intention to file any motion in respect of a site visit. We simply put it onto our list. If Your Honours felt that it would be useful for you to see, if not all, at least some of the areas in real life, then the Defence and Prosecution are in agreement that we feel it may well be useful, if I can put it that way. We have no intention of filing a motion and adding to the already lengthy list of motions. This is -- can I put it, this is an agreed, as it were, application by the Defence, if Your Honours felt it was necessary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: I hear what you are saying, but I would have thought that the initiative should come from counsel rather than from the Chamber. We are probably agreed in the result. It's only a question of, for whatever reason, from whom the initiative should come. We don't --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, the initiative is coming jointly from Prosecution and Defence counsel, but we really don't feel that it requires another motion. We feel -- can I put it this way, and I'm sure I'll be corrected by Defence counsel if I put it inadequately or wrongly, that it may well be of assistance to Your Honours if Your Honours say so, if you see what I mean. It's a matter for Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Of course it is, but do I -- when we talk about a motion, do I understand the position to be that you are now so moving?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry. I thought you meant yet another written motion. We are -- we are making the application for Your Honours to undertake a site visit, the organisation of which is quite complicated, so it needs to be worked out in advance, so that Your Honours may see for yourselves the actual areas that this case is concerned with, or at least some of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Okay. So the office for the Prosecution now having moved, so moved, and counsel for the Defence not object -- Yes, Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: Well, I believe Ms. Korner explained that it is a joint application by both Defence and the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Yes, I followed that. I was presuming to articulate your position.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, Your Honours. I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. PANTELIC
utterances.text: That is correct, Your Honours. Just for the record, we are also concurring with this application.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: The only practical question remaining is that the Chamber would need to know where it is proposed that the site visit take us. But the motion having been made in open court, the Chamber would formally rule at the appropriate time. But we understand the joint position of both sides in this regard. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I have a feeling that to cover every single municipality would be a fairly lengthy and difficult task, so I think the best thing is that the Defence and Prosecution sit down together and work out which of the municipalities which we feel you should see. I mean, the ARK ones are all grouped very close together, but the others are more widespread. But, Your Honour, if we can get back to you with an agreed list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. As regards item 2, outstanding motions, we thank you for the lists that we got a few hours ago, and these matters would be -- are all in process, and the rulings would -- there is nothing that we can practically say today.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honours. And I know this is a recurring theme, particularly from me, but I'm afraid I must ask Your Honours to rule today on the Prosecution's motion for safe conduct for Witness ST-187 which was filed on the 23rd of December, and it's consented to. There's no objection from the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: That draft has been prepared, and the order will be made today or, by the latest, on Monday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. And, Your Honour, in relation to that -- to the outstanding matters, can I just make one observation. It's the adjudicated facts as against -- which have been granted in respect of Stanisic, but have not yet been granted, if they're going to be, as against Zupljanin. And the difficulty with not having a ruling is that it raises the question of what evidence the Prosecution will be obliged to call. And the longer this is outstanding, the more complicated it becomes, because we're dealing with municipalities now where we're not calling -- for example, Kljuc, we're calling very little evidence because of the adjudicated facts, but they've only been granted as against Stanisic, and Kljuc really affects Zupljanin more than it does Stanisic, to a great extent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: You would appreciate, of course, that is an exercise which is very labour intensive, and it is nearly complete. I can certainly say that much. And it probably wouldn't be prudent for me to say anything further than that. But one of the complicating factors had been the joinder since the initial application had been made, and also you'll bear in mind that the decision is now being rendered by your Bench which has only been constituted since September.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I fully understand, I do, Your Honour, we really do, but I'm afraid we think that a motion that has been outstanding for nearly two years as of next week is something that requires urgent, urgent attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE DELVOIE
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, let me just add that for the moment, the Judges' time out of court is practically -- for 95 per cent devoted to adjudicated facts, to that motion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. All right. I don't think I can say anything further on our list. Your Honours, number 3, while I'm on my feet, if I can just explain what that means. Judge Harhoff -- Your Honours, there's still confusion about the policy and the criteria for the admission of the documents, and His Honour Judge Harhoff, on the 9th of December, indicated that he would provide -- I'm so sorry, the Trial Chamber would provide guide-lines which would be sent to counsel first before they were issued in draft. The difficulty, for example, is -- can I take a very simple example. The newspaper articles. There doesn't appear, to us, to be a policy on this. In some cases, they're admitted. In other cases, because they're newspaper articles, an objection is raised and they're not admitted. And we really -- we really would like, if it's at all possible, to have written guide-lines which we can all understand and follow as to how documents will be admitted. The other matter is, of course, this business where we have a number of documents, for example, intercepts or records of meetings, where we don't have enough time to go through each and every one with the witness, whether we can have those admitted, as it were, as part of a bulk exhibit. And so all we're asking for or reminding Your Honours is that if guide-lines could be drafted and issued in draft, and then we'll all know where we are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: It is something that, as you indicated, Judge Harhoff has alerted you that an attempt will be made, but I will say in this context something that I've expressed privately, and that is that over the years that the Tribunal has been in existence, and the jurisprudence and practice that has developed, the fact that this still is an issue means that any attempt that is made to deal with an issue like this comprehensively is going to be futile in the sense that there will still be opportunities for argument and submissions. So on a case-by-case basis, the practical result is likely to be that the -- whereas general principles can be stated, that it is only going to be resolved on a case-by-case basis. And in that vein I don't know what was intended by item 4, but what I just said would also applied to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We'll see.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And, Your Honours, item number 5 I'll get Ms. Pidwell to deal with, because I make a mess every time I deal with MFIs.

utterances.speaker: MS. PIDWELL
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's simply a technical matter that you may recall there were five MFI documents that were left over from when Dr. Donia gave his evidence, and they were MFI'd on the basis that it was unclear whether they were within the boundaries of the Sarajevo report that you partially admitted. Upon review, it appears that one was actually on our 65 ter list all along. It had a different ERN number and so had slipped through the cracks. And so that one we're asking to be formally admitted now on the record because it was in our 65 ter list and was simply MFI'd previously. It's P14, and it was 65 ter number 903. And it was our fault, and we're very sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: So that document is now admitted and assigned the relevant number by the Registry.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: It will remain Exhibit P14, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: Thank you. So we take the adjournment now until Monday -- sorry, where are we on Monday; here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: We resume at 9.00 a.m. on Monday in Courtroom III. So I wish everyone a safe weekend. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HALL
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 25th day of January, 2010, at 9.00 a.m. 22 23 24 25
